sections.title: The hook
sections.intro_md:
In the south of Loktak Lake, islands drift. They are not made of rock or sand but of matted grass, roots and rotting plants, some a metre or two thick, and a man can walk on them, build a hut on them, and fish from them. On the biggest stretch of these floating mats, 40 square kilometres of it, lives a deer found nowhere else in the wild. It steps so carefully on the spongy ground that people call it the dancing deer.

An hour's drive north, in Imphal, there is a market run only by women, older than the British in India, and a polo ground where the game the British took to the world was being played long before they arrived. The same small state gave India Mary Kom, Mirabai Chanu and a classical dance in which no one wears ankle bells.

Manipur is also, since May 2023, a place split by a conflict between its valley and its hills. Today you learn both: the beauty and the fault line.

sections.title: Manipur at a glance
sections.intro_md:
Manipur is a small state on India's far eastern edge, shaped like an oval bowl: a flat valley in the middle, ringed by ranges of hills. It borders Nagaland to the north, Assam to the west, Mizoram to the south-west and Myanmar to the east and south.

It covers **22,327 km²**, a little bigger than Mizoram, and had **28.56 lakh** people in the 2011 census. The **Imphal Valley** is only about **1,800 km²**, roughly 8% of the land, yet the valley districts held **57%** of the people in 2011. The hills, 92% of the land, are home to dozens of tribes, grouped broadly as Naga and Kuki-Zo. The valley belongs mostly to the **Meitei**, whose language, Meiteilon or Manipuri, is the state's official language.

Manipur was a kingdom for close to two thousand years by its own chronicle. It joined India on **15 October 1949**, became a Union Territory in 1956 and a full state on **21 January 1972**. It now has **16 districts** and a 60-seat assembly.

sections.title: A bowl of hills with a lake at its heart
sections.intro_md:
Picture Manipur as a saucer. The flat floor is the Imphal Valley, about 800 metres above sea level, laid down by rivers that once filled it as a lake. Around it rise ranges of hills running north to south, steep and forested, reaching about 2,994 metres at Mount Iso (Tenipu) on the Nagaland border.

Two river systems drain the state. The Imphal (Manipur) River runs south through the valley, past Loktak, into Myanmar, where its waters reach the Chindwin. The Barak flows west through the hills into Assam and Bangladesh. That split matters: the valley looks east to Myanmar as much as west to India.

The wildlife here is a meeting of Indian, Chinese and Southeast Asian species: hoolock gibbons, Mrs Hume's pheasant (the state bird, called nongin), and the sangai on its floating home.

spotlights.name: Loktak Lake
spotlights.spot_it: A shallow lake dotted with round green rings and floating islands, with thatched huts sitting on the islands.
spotlights.story_md: Loktak is the largest freshwater lake in North-East India. It is a pulsing lake: its surface shrinks to about 250 km² in the dry months and swells to around 500 km² in the rains, with a typical area of about 287 km². Rivers from the valley drain into it and one barrage at Ithai, built for the Loktak hydropower project in 1983, now controls its outflow. The lake was listed as a Ramsar wetland in 1990, then put on the Montreux Record of threatened wetlands in 1993 because silt, nutrients and the fixed water level were choking it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Loktak feeds Manipur's fish, power and water, and holds the floating islands that make it unique.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lake that breathes: half its size in winter, double in the rains.

spotlights.name: Phumdis, the floating islands
spotlights.spot_it: Thick floating mats of grass and roots, often cut into perfect circles by fishermen.
spotlights.story_md: A phumdi is a heap of vegetation, soil and organic matter, held together by roots, that floats. About four-fifths of its mass sits under water, like an iceberg. In the dry season, when the water drops, a phumdi touches the lake bed and its roots soak up nutrients; when the rains come it lifts off again. Fishermen build huts called phumsangs on them and cut phumdis into rings, called athaphum, to trap fish inside. The trouble: the barrage keeps the water high all year, so phumdis can no longer touch bottom, and many are thinning and breaking up.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Phumdis are the habitat of the sangai and the fishing grounds of thousands of families.
spotlights.memory_hook: Islands that float like icebergs: four-fifths under water.

spotlights.name: Keibul Lamjao National Park
spotlights.spot_it: A tawny plain of reeds and grass on water at the south end of Loktak.
spotlights.story_md: Keibul Lamjao is the only floating national park in the world. Its 40 km² are mostly one great phumdi, thickest in the middle, where the grass grows tall enough to hide a deer. It began as a sanctuary in 1966 and became a national park in 1977, created for one animal, the sangai. A small hill, Pabot, and a watchtower give visitors the best chance of seeing the herd at dawn. Because the ground floats, rangers patrol by boat, and a fire in the dry season can burn the floor of the park itself.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the last wild home of the sangai, and a habitat made of floating plants.
spotlights.memory_hook: A national park you could, in theory, tow away.

spotlights.name: Sangai, the dancing deer
spotlights.spot_it: A slim brown deer whose antlers sweep forward in one long curve from the brow, like a bow.
spotlights.story_md: The sangai is Manipur's state animal, a subspecies of Eld's deer with brow-antlers that run forward over the face and then curve up. It walks on the floating phumdi by placing its weight gently, which gives it a delicate, hopping gait: the dancing deer. By 1950 it was thought extinct. In 1953 a naturalist found six. Careful protection brought the count to 204 in 2013 and 260 in a 2016 census by the forest department, Manipur University and the Wildlife Institute of India. Every wild sangai alive lives in one 40 km² park, so one fire, flood or disease could end the species in the wild.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A whole subspecies hangs on one floating park.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six deer in 1953, all the sangai on earth on one floating mat.

spotlights.name: Shirui lily
spotlights.spot_it: A pale pink, bell-shaped lily, hanging its head on a hillside of grass, in May and June.
spotlights.story_md: The Shirui lily grows wild on one place on earth: the upper slopes of Shirui Kashong peak in Ukhrul district. The plant hunter Frank Kingdon-Ward found it in 1946 and named it Lilium mackliniae, after his wife Jean Macklin. Grown in Britain from his seed, it won an Award of Merit from the Royal Horticultural Society in 1948. The Tangkhul Naga people of Shirui tell of a goddess who lives on the peak, and the lily is her flower. It is Manipur's state flower, and the Shirui Lily Festival each spring brings visitors up the mountain.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the rarest wild lilies in the world, and a symbol of the hill districts.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lily that lives on one hill and was named for a wife.

spotlights.name: Dzükou Valley
spotlights.spot_it: A high green valley of rolling, cropped bamboo-grass hills with a stream winding through.
spotlights.story_md: Dzükou sits on the border of Manipur and Nagaland at about 2,400 metres. In summer the dwarf bamboo that covers it looks like mown lawn from a distance; in June and July the Dzükou lily, a different species from the Shirui lily, blooms on the slopes. Trekkers usually walk in from the Nagaland side near Kohima. The valley's ownership has long been argued over by the two states and by the Mao Naga and Southern Angami communities, and fires on its slopes in recent winters have drawn both states' firefighters.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A shared, and disputed, highland that shows how state lines cut across hill peoples.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lawn of bamboo at 2,400 metres that two states both call home.

sections.title: Who lives here: valley and hills
sections.intro_md:
Manipur has three big groups, and the land is split between them very unevenly.

The **Meitei** are the majority, a little over half the population, and live mostly in the Imphal Valley. Their kingdom built Imphal, their language is the state language, and most are Hindu, with a strong revival of the older Sanamahi faith. **Meitei Pangals**, Muslims who settled from the 17th century, are about 8% of the state.

The hills belong to many tribes, grouped as **Naga** (Tangkhul, Mao, Poumai, Maram, Zeliangrong and others) in the north and east and **Kuki-Zo** (Thadou, Paite, Hmar, Vaiphei and others) mostly in the south and west. Most are Christian. In the 2011 census Hindus were 41.4% and Christians 41.3%: Manipur is almost exactly split.

The key rule to understand today: land in the hills is protected for tribes, so Meiteis cannot buy it, while hill people can buy land in the valley. Much of the anger since 2023 runs through that rule.

spotlights.name: Ukhrul and the Tangkhul Naga
spotlights.spot_it: A hill town strung along a ridge, churches on the skyline, at about 1,800 metres.
spotlights.story_md: Ukhrul is the heart of the Tangkhul Naga, one of the largest Naga peoples of Manipur. The town sits on a ridge with views east toward Myanmar. Tangkhul villages are known for Longpi black pottery, the Kachai lemon, the Hathei chilli of Sirarakhong and the Shirui lily. Most Tangkhuls are Baptist Christians; the American missionary William Pettigrew opened a school in Ukhrul in 1896, and literacy and church life spread together. Their great festival is Luira Phanit, the seed-sowing feast, in early spring.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The hill districts are not a blank around the valley: each has its own language, faith and produce.
spotlights.memory_hook: One ridge town, four famous products: pots, lemons, chillies, lilies.

spotlights.name: Churachandpur
spotlights.spot_it: A busy hill town south-west of Loktak, the largest in the Kuki-Zo hills.
spotlights.story_md: Churachandpur, known to many of its residents as Lamka, is the main town of the Kuki-Zo peoples of southern Manipur: Thadou, Paite, Hmar, Vaiphei, Zou, Simte and others, related by language to the Mizo and the Chin of Myanmar. It is named after Maharaja Churachand Singh, the king the British put on the throne in 1891. Mary Kom grew up in a village in this district. Since 2023, with the valley closed to its people, Churachandpur has had to reach the rest of India by the long road through Mizoram, and it has become a centre of the Kuki-Zo demand for a separate administration.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The town shows the conflict's geography: a hill society cut off from the valley capital.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lamka: the Kuki-Zo capital in all but name.

sections.title: Kangleipak: the kingdom
sections.intro_md:
Before it was Manipur, the land had other names: **Kangleipak**, Meitrabak, Sanaleibak. Seven Meitei clans, the salais, merged over centuries under the Ningthouja dynasty, which ruled from Kangla.

The kingdom sat between two worlds. Its kings fought and married into the Burmese and Shan courts to the east, and traded and prayed with Bengal and Assam to the west. In the 18th century the court turned to Vaishnav Hinduism. Under **Bhagyachandra** (reigned on and off from 1759 to 1798) that faith produced the Ras Lila dance and the temple of Govindaji.

The worst memory is the **Seven Years Devastation**, Chahi Taret Khuntakpa, from 1819 to 1826, when a Burmese invasion emptied the valley. The British helped expel the Burmese in the First Anglo-Burmese War, and the treaty of Yandabo in 1826 recognised Manipur's king. That help came with a price, paid in 1891.

spotlights.name: Cheitharol Kumbaba, the royal chronicle
spotlights.spot_it: Old handwritten pages of Meitei script recording each year of a reign.
spotlights.story_md: The Cheitharol Kumbaba is the court chronicle of the Meitei kings. It opens with King Nongda Lairen Pakhangba, who by its count took the throne in 33 CE, and lists kings, wars, fires, eclipses, floods and festivals year by year down to the end of the monarchy in the 20th century. Historians treat the earliest centuries with caution, since the entries for them were likely written down much later. From about the 15th century onward the record is detailed and often matches outside sources. Few states in India have a home-grown year-by-year record this long.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gives Manipur a written memory of itself stretching back nearly two thousand years.
spotlights.memory_hook: A royal diary that claims to start in 33 CE.

spotlights.name: Kangla, the old palace
spotlights.spot_it: A walled, moated enclosure in central Imphal, with a golden-roofed gate, green lawns and two white dragon-lions.
spotlights.story_md: Kangla, meaning roughly 'dry land', was the seat of Meitei kings and the most sacred site of the Meitei faith. After the war of 1891 the British took it over, and after independence it stayed a military base, latterly the headquarters of the Assam Rifles. In 2004, after mass protests over the killing of Thangjam Manorama in Assam Rifles custody, the Centre handed Kangla back to the state on 20 November 2004. It is now a heritage park with museums, a boathouse for royal racing boats and the restored Kangla Sha statues.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Who holds Kangla has always meant who holds Manipur.
spotlights.memory_hook: 113 years of soldiers, then handed back after a protest.

spotlights.name: Kangla Sha
spotlights.spot_it: A huge white guardian beast with a lion's body, a dragon's head and curling horns, standing at Kangla.
spotlights.story_md: The Kangla Sha is a mythical creature of Meitei belief, part lion and part dragon, the royal emblem and guardian of Kangla. A pair stood in front of the coronation hall. After defeating Manipur in 1891, the British blew them up, an act still remembered as an insult. The figures were rebuilt much later, and today the Kangla Sha appears on state symbols and logos, from the state police to sports teams. Small models stand outside homes and offices as protectors.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the single most recognisable symbol of Meitei kingship.
spotlights.memory_hook: Blown up by the British in 1891, rebuilt in stone and pride.

spotlights.name: Pamheiba (Garib Niwaz)
spotlights.spot_it: An 18th-century king remembered under a Persian title, 'kind to the poor'.
spotlights.story_md: Pamheiba ruled from 1709 to 1748 and turned Manipur into a regional power, raiding deep into Burma. He also changed its faith: under the influence of a preacher from Sylhet, Shantidas Gosai, he adopted Ramanandi Vaishnavism and made it the court religion, taking the name Garib Niwaz. Tradition holds that in 1732 he ordered the old Meitei scriptures, the puyas, to be gathered and burned, an event called Puya Meithaba. Historians argue about how many were burned and whether the story is exact, but for Sanamahi revivalists it is a founding wound.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is why Hinduism became the faith of most Meitei, and why some now reject that change.
spotlights.memory_hook: A king who won wars in Burma and, it is said, burned his own books.

spotlights.name: Vishnu temple, Bishnupur
spotlights.spot_it: A small square brick temple with a rounded, curving roof, standing in a garden.
spotlights.story_md: At Bishnupur, 27 km south of Imphal, stands a brick temple built in 1467 under King Kiyamba to house an image of Vishnu that, by tradition, was a gift from a Shan king of the Pong kingdom across the hills. It is one of the oldest surviving buildings in Manipur, small and made of thin bricks, with a rounded, curving roof quite unlike the tall stone spires of temples in Odisha or Tamil Nadu. The town, once called Lamangdong, took its later name from the temple.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proves Vishnu was worshipped in Manipur centuries before the 18th-century conversion.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Vishnu that came over the eastern hills, from a Shan king.

sections.title: From kingdom to Indian state: 1891 to 1972
sections.intro_md:
After 1891 the British kept Manipur's kings but ran its affairs through a political agent. They installed a five-year-old boy, Churachand Singh, on the throne, abolished the old Meitei labour system only slowly, and kept the hills under separate rule. That split between a valley governed through the king and hills governed directly by the British is one root of today's divide.

Two women's uprisings, in 1904 and 1939, showed how politics in Manipur worked. Then came the Second World War, which arrived at Imphal itself.

In 1949 the kingdom merged with India. Manipur became a Union Territory in 1956 and a full state on 21 January 1972, along with Meghalaya and Tripura. From the 1960s armed groups emerged in the valley and hills; the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act of 1958 was applied to the state, and with it came decades of protest.

spotlights.name: The Anglo-Manipur War, 1891
spotlights.spot_it: A short war in spring 1891 that ended with the Union Jack over Kangla.
spotlights.story_md: It began as a palace quarrel. In 1890 the prince and army chief Tikendrajit Singh ousted his brother the king. The British, who wanted Tikendrajit punished, sent the Chief Commissioner of Assam, James Quinton, with 400 Gurkhas. An attempt to arrest Tikendrajit in March 1891 failed, fighting broke out, and Quinton and four other British officials who went to negotiate were killed. Three British columns then marched in from Kohima, Silchar and Tamu. After the last stand at Khongjom in late April, Imphal fell on 27 April 1891. Manipur became a princely state under British control.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ended Manipur's independence: 1891 is the line between the kingdom and the colonial era.
spotlights.memory_hook: A palace quarrel, five dead officials, and a kingdom lost in five weeks.

spotlights.name: Bir Tikendrajit Singh
spotlights.spot_it: A young prince in a turban, hero of 1891; Imphal airport now carries his name.
spotlights.story_md: Tikendrajit was the Senapati, army commander, of Manipur, and a popular figure known for his horsemanship and polo. After the war he was captured, tried and publicly hanged on 13 August 1891, together with Thangal General, at a spot in Imphal now called Bir Tikendrajit Park. Manipur keeps 13 August as Patriots' Day. His portrait hangs in the Parliament of India, and Imphal's airport is now named Bir Tikendrajit International Airport. Khongjom Day, in April, honours the soldiers of the war's last battle.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He turned a defeat into a founding story of Manipuri patriotism.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hanged in public on 13 August 1891; now the name on your boarding pass.

spotlights.name: Nupi Lan, the women's wars
spotlights.spot_it: Thousands of women in phaneks crowding the streets of Imphal around British officers.
spotlights.story_md: Nupi Lan means 'women's war', and Manipur had two. In 1904 the British ordered men to fetch timber from the Kabaw valley to rebuild an officer's burnt bungalow, reviving the hated lalup system of unpaid labour. More than 5,000 women protested until the order was withdrawn. In 1939, during a scarcity, merchants were exporting rice while people went hungry. On 12 December 1939, market women surrounded the political agent and forced a halt to rice exports. The protest grew into a movement for political reform. 12 December is Nupi Lan Day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the roots of women's public power in Manipur, from Ima Keithel to the Meira Paibi.
spotlights.memory_hook: When the men were sent away, the market women went to war.

spotlights.name: The merger of 1949
spotlights.spot_it: A short agreement signed in Shillong, which ended the monarchy.
spotlights.story_md: In 1947 Manipur adopted its own constitution, the Manipur State Constitution Act, and in 1948 it held elections with universal adult franchise, before India itself did. Then, on 21 September 1949, Maharaja Bodhachandra Singh signed a merger agreement in Shillong, where he had gone for talks. It took effect on 15 October 1949, and Manipur became a Part C state of India, run by a Chief Commissioner. Many in Manipur argue the king had no authority to sign without the elected assembly, which was dissolved; some groups mark 15 October as a black day. The question still shapes politics in the valley.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why a part of Manipur's armed politics questions how it joined India.
spotlights.memory_hook: An elected assembly in 1948, dissolved by a signature in 1949.

sections.title: When the Second World War came to Imphal
sections.intro_md:
For the people of Manipur, 1944 is **Japan Laan**, the Japanese war. For four months the valley was a battlefield between the Japanese 15th Army, with the Indian National Army alongside it, and the British 14th Army under William Slim.

The Japanese plan was bold and doomed. Mutaguchi's men carried three weeks of food and expected to live off captured stocks. Instead the Allies flew in supplies, and the siege broke the Japanese army in Burma. Imphal and Kohima together are often called the 'Stalingrad of the East'. One early stand mattered a great deal: at Sangshak, in Ukhrul district, the 50th Indian Parachute Brigade held up a Japanese division for about a week in March 1944, buying time for Kohima and Imphal.

Villagers paid heavily: fields burned, homes shelled, men pressed into labour by both sides. Japanese pilgrims and bone-collectors still visit, and old helmets and shells still turn up in the hills.

spotlights.name: The Battle of Imphal, 1944
spotlights.spot_it: Allied soldiers and transport planes in the hills around Imphal, March to July 1944.
spotlights.story_md: In March 1944 Japan's 15th Army under Lieutenant General Renya Mutaguchi crossed from Burma to seize Imphal and its supply base, a plan called Operation U-Go. They surrounded the town, but the Allies flew in men, food and ammunition to Imphal's airstrips while the siege held. The Japanese, who had counted on capturing British supplies, starved. By July they retreated in the monsoon. Japan's losses at Imphal and Kohima together came to 54,879 casualties, including 13,376 dead, most from hunger and disease; the Allies lost 12,603. In 2013 a British National Army Museum poll voted Imphal and Kohima Britain's greatest battle.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the turning point of the war in Burma, fought in Manipur's paddy fields.
spotlights.memory_hook: The army that planned to eat the enemy's food starved instead.

spotlights.name: INA flag at Moirang
spotlights.spot_it: A memorial complex in Moirang with a statue of Subhas Chandra Bose and a museum.
spotlights.story_md: On 14 April 1944, during the Japanese advance, officers of Subhas Chandra Bose's Indian National Army, which fought alongside Japan, raised the INA tricolour at Moirang, near Loktak. It was one of the first places on Indian soil where that flag flew. The INA Memorial Complex at Moirang now holds letters, photographs, badges and weapons of the INA, and a statue of Bose. It is a reminder that for some Indians in 1944 the war was a fight against the British, not alongside them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ties a small Manipuri town to the story of India's independence.
spotlights.memory_hook: Moirang: where an Indian flag flew while Imphal was still British.

spotlights.name: Red Hill and the Imphal Peace Museum
spotlights.spot_it: A small hill south of Imphal with a Japanese memorial and a modern museum beside it.
spotlights.story_md: Maibam Lokpaching, called Red Hill by the British, was the site of some of the bitterest fighting in May 1944. Japanese veterans and families built a peace memorial here. In June 2019 the Imphal Peace Museum opened beside it, funded by Japan's Nippon Foundation and run with local partners, telling the battle through the eyes of Manipuri villagers who lost homes, fields and lives to both armies. Japanese groups still come to search for remains of soldiers who never went home.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It tells the war from the side of people who never chose it.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hill named for its blood, now a museum of peace.

spotlights.name: Imphal War Cemetery
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of low bronze plaques on stone, lined up on a mown lawn.
spotlights.story_md: The Commonwealth War Graves Commission keeps two cemeteries in Imphal: the Imphal War Cemetery and the Imphal Indian Army War Cemetery. Together they hold the graves and cremation memorials of thousands of British, Indian, Gurkha and African soldiers who died in the siege. The grounds are quiet, green and carefully kept, a few minutes from the busy centre of the city.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where the global war became local graves.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bronze names on a lawn in the middle of Imphal.

sections.title: Meiteilon and many tongues
sections.intro_md:
The state language is **Meiteilon**, also called Manipuri, a Tibeto-Burman language spoken as a mother tongue by about 1.76 million people in India in 2011, about 1.5 million of them in Manipur. Meiteis of the Barak valley in Assam, of Tripura and of Bangladesh speak it too. It entered the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution on 20 August 1992, which is now celebrated as Manipuri Language Day.

Around it are dozens of hill languages: Tangkhul, Thadou, Paite, Mao, Rongmei, Hmar and many more. Many are so different that villages a valley apart use Meiteilon, Hindi or English to speak to each other. English is widely spoken in the hills, a legacy of mission schools.

Meiteilon has a long literature. Its classic texts were written on paper made from bark and kept in old families as puyas. Modern Manipuri poetry and theatre are among the most active in India's North-East.

spotlights.name: Meitei Mayek, the script named after the body
spotlights.spot_it: Rounded letters with no headline, often seen on signboards and number plates in Imphal.
spotlights.story_md: Meitei Mayek is Manipur's own script. Each letter is named after a part of the human body: the first, kok, means head; the second, sam, means hair; the third, lai, means forehead, and so on. From the 18th century, with Vaishnavism, the Bengali script replaced it for most writing. A revival movement brought it back: it entered school textbooks in the 2000s, and in 2022 Meitei language newspapers agreed to switch from Bengali to Meitei script from 15 January 2023. It has 27 main letters, 18 original ones plus 9 added for borrowed sounds.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Getting its script back is a central part of Meitei identity today.
spotlights.memory_hook: An alphabet you could draw on your own body: head, hair, forehead.

spotlights.name: Khamba and Thoibi
spotlights.spot_it: A pair of lovers from Moirang, told in songs and the Khamba Thoibi duet dance.
spotlights.story_md: Manipur's great love story comes from the Moirang kingdom on the shore of Loktak. Khamba, an orphan from a poor family, loves Thoibi, the king's daughter. Her father and a rival, Nongban, set him impossible tasks: Khamba must catch a wild bull with his bare hands and kill a tiger. Thoibi is exiled for defying her father. In the end they marry, but the story ends with Khamba killed by mistake by the one he loved. The tale is sung by bards called pena players and danced at Lai Haraoba in Moirang.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the Romeo and Juliet of Manipur, rooted in a real lakeside town.
spotlights.memory_hook: A man who wrestled a bull for a princess.

sections.title: Faith: old gods, Krishna and the church
sections.intro_md:
Religion in Manipur has layers. The oldest is **Sanamahism**, the Meitei faith of ancestor and nature gods: Sanamahi, the household god kept in the south-west corner of every Meitei home, Leimarel Sidabi, the household goddess, and hundreds of local umang lai in sacred groves. Its priests and priestesses, the maibas and maibis, still lead rituals.

From the 18th century the Meitei court took up **Gaudiya Vaishnavism**, the Krishna devotion of Bengal. Meitei Hindus wear the white tilak on the nose and forehead, and Krishna stories fill the dance. Yet they kept many old gods, and today a strong revival movement reclaims Sanamahism and the old script.

In the hills, American Baptist and other missionaries arrived from the 1890s. Within a century most Naga and Kuki-Zo people had become **Christian**, and churches now crown nearly every hill village.

spotlights.name: Lai Haraoba
spotlights.spot_it: White-clad priestesses in slow, swaying dance before a shrine, with a pena fiddle playing.
spotlights.story_md: Lai Haraoba means 'the merrymaking of the gods'. It is the great ritual festival of the Meitei faith, held at shrines of the umang lai, the forest and ancestral deities of each locality, mostly in spring. Over days or weeks the maibis, priestesses, call the god up from the water, and dancers act out the creation of the world, the building of a house, the planting of cotton and the weaving of cloth, through more than 300 hand gestures. The festival ends with games, wrestling and the Khamba Thoibi dance in Moirang.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the oldest living layer of Manipur's culture, and the root of its classical dance.
spotlights.memory_hook: A festival where the dance teaches you how the world was made.

spotlights.name: Shree Govindajee Temple
spotlights.spot_it: A white temple with two gold domes beside the old palace in Imphal, its hall filled with dancers at festivals.
spotlights.story_md: Govindaji is Krishna, and his temple next to the royal palace in Imphal is the centre of Meitei Vaishnav life. Tradition says King Bhagyachandra saw in a dream an image of Krishna carved from a jackfruit tree on Kaina hill, and had it made. The present temple, with twin gold-plated domes and a large open hall, the mandapa, hosts the big Ras Lila performances on autumn full moons. The palace grounds also hold the Bijoy Govinda moat where the Heikru Hidongba boat race takes place.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where Manipur's Vaishnav faith and its classical dance meet.
spotlights.memory_hook: Krishna, carved from a jackfruit tree a king dreamed of.

sections.title: Dance, drum, sword and stage
sections.intro_md:
Almost every art in Manipur begins at the Lai Haraoba shrine and grows through the Vaishnav temple. The same body trains in all of them: a Manipuri dancer learns Thang-Ta, a drummer learns to leap, an actor learns both.

**Manipuri dance** is one of the eight forms the Sangeet Natak Akademi counts as classical. Its Ras Lila performances fill the Govindaji temple on the autumn and spring full moons. **Nata Sankirtana**, singing and drumming for Krishna, is part of nearly every Meitei life event and is on UNESCO's world heritage list.

Manipur's **theatre** is famous across India. Directors like Ratan Thiyam and Heisnam Kanhailal used body, breath and ritual instead of words. Kanhailal's *Draupadi* (2000), in which the actor Heisnam Sabitri strips on stage in protest, became one of Indian theatre's most debated moments.

spotlights.name: Manipuri Ras Lila
spotlights.spot_it: Dancers in stiff, barrel-shaped skirts covered in mirrors, gliding without a sound, a veil over the face.
spotlights.story_md: Manipuri is one of India's classical dance forms, and its heart is the Ras Lila, the circle dance of Krishna and the gopis. Tradition says King Bhagyachandra dreamed the whole dance, costume included, and first staged it in 1779 with his daughter Bimbavati as Radha. The women wear the potloi, a stiff cylindrical skirt decorated with mirrors and sequins, and a fine veil. Movements are round and soft, like waves; the feet never stamp and dancers wear no ankle bells. In 1919 Rabindranath Tagore saw Manipuri dance in Sylhet and brought a teacher to Santiniketan, which carried it across India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the gentlest of India's classical dances, and Manipur's best-known art.
spotlights.memory_hook: The dance a king dreamed, with no bells and no stamping.

spotlights.name: Pung Cholom
spotlights.spot_it: Men in white turbans drumming barrel drums while leaping and spinning in the air.
spotlights.story_md: The pung is a two-headed barrel drum, and pung cholom is the dance of its drummers. Wearing white dhotis and turbans, they play complex rhythms while whirling, crouching and jumping, sometimes landing in a squat without missing a beat. It opens Nata Sankirtana, the devotional singing and drumming performed at Meitei temples and at life events from a child's ear-piercing to a funeral. In 2013 UNESCO inscribed Sankirtana of Manipur on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a performance where the musicians are also the dancers and the acrobats.
spotlights.memory_hook: Drummers who fly while they play.

spotlights.name: Thang-Ta
spotlights.spot_it: Two fighters with sword and shield, or sword and spear, moving in low crouches and fast circles.
spotlights.story_md: Thang-Ta, 'sword and spear', is the martial art of the Meitei, part of a wider system called Huyen Langlon. It trains breath, footwork and weapons in a way close to dance, and dancers of Manipuri learn from it. After the war of 1891 the British banned it, and it survived in secret. It was revived after independence, is taught in academies across Imphal, and was added to the Khelo India Youth Games among the indigenous sports, alongside gatka and kalaripayattu.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It links Manipur's fighting past to its dance and sport today.
spotlights.memory_hook: Banned by the British, kept alive in courtyards.

spotlights.name: Ratan Thiyam
spotlights.spot_it: His theatre campus in Imphal, and on stage, huge slow pictures made of light, colour, chant and drumming.
spotlights.story_md: Ratan Thiyam founded the Chorus Repertory Theatre in Imphal in 1976 and became one of the world's best-known Indian stage directors. His plays, such as Chakravyuha (1984) about the death of Abhimanyu, and Uttar Priyadarshi (1996), mixed Manipuri martial arts, ritual and Sanskrit drama into slow, stunning images. Chakravyuha won a Fringe First at Edinburgh in 1987. He received the Padma Shri in 1989 and later chaired the National School of Drama. He died in Imphal on 23 July 2025, aged 77.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He put Manipur on the stages of the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: The director who painted with bodies and light.

spotlights.name: Ishanou, the film
spotlights.spot_it: A 1990 Manipuri film about a young mother called away by the goddess to become a maibi.
spotlights.story_md: Aribam Syam Sharma's Ishanou, 'the chosen one', tells of Tampha, a wife and mother who is seized by the spirit of the goddess and must leave her family to join the maibis, the priestesses of Lai Haraoba. It was selected for the Un Certain Regard section at Cannes in 1991, a rare honour for a film from India's North-East. A restored print returned to Cannes in its Classics section in 2023. Sharma's earlier film Imagi Ningthem (1981) won the top prize at the Festival of Three Continents in Nantes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Manipuri cinema reached the world's top festivals decades before Indian regional film became fashionable.
spotlights.memory_hook: A film about a woman claimed by a goddess, shown twice at Cannes.

sections.title: Where polo was born
sections.intro_md:
Manipur's claim to fame in world sport is simple and well documented: modern polo comes from here. British officers in Cachar learned it from Manipuri players in the 1850s and carried it to Calcutta, England and then the Americas and Argentina.

In the Meitei world, the game is sacred. Marjing is its god. Kings played it, and so did Tikendrajit. Polo also needs a pony, and the small, tough Manipuri pony is part of the story.

Manipur's other traditional sports are just as distinctive: **mukna**, belt wrestling that ends Lai Haraoba; **yubi lakpi**, coconut rugby; **khong kangjei**, hockey on foot; and **hiyang tannaba**, the boat race. They train bodies that later win medals in modern sport.

spotlights.name: Sagol Kangjei, Manipuri polo
spotlights.spot_it: Riders on small ponies with long cane sticks, chasing a bamboo-root ball across a grass field; leg guards and turbans.
spotlights.story_md: Sagol kangjei, 'horse hockey', is the Meitei game that became modern polo. In the old form there were no goalposts: a goal was scored by hitting the ball over the back line, and teams of seven played on small ponies. Kings and nobles played, and so did villagers. In 1859 British planters and officers in Cachar, led by Lieutenant Joseph Sherer, learned the game from Manipuri players and founded the Silchar Polo Club, the first modern polo club. Calcutta followed in 1862, then England in 1869. Sherer is often called the father of modern polo; the game he learned was Manipur's.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The world's game of kings was borrowed from Manipur.
spotlights.memory_hook: Polo came to Britain from a Manipuri pony's saddle.

spotlights.name: Mapal Kangjeibung
spotlights.spot_it: A long grass field in central Imphal, bordered by stands, next to the palace grounds.
spotlights.story_md: Mapal Kangjeibung, the polo ground in Imphal, is often called the oldest polo ground in the world still in use. Sagol kangjei has been played on this spot for centuries. Today it hosts the Manipur Statehood Day Polo Tournament and the international polo tournament held during the Sangai Festival, where teams from abroad play on Manipuri ponies.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It lets you stand on the ground where polo history began.
spotlights.memory_hook: The world's oldest polo field is in the middle of Imphal.

spotlights.name: Manipuri pony
spotlights.spot_it: A small, sturdy horse, around 11 to 13 hands high, with a big head and quick feet.
spotlights.story_md: The Manipuri pony is a small native breed, said to descend from Mongolian wild horses crossed with Arab stock. It carried Meitei cavalry, which was feared by the Burmese, and it is the original polo pony. In the Second World War it served both armies. Today numbers have fallen sharply as farmland swallowed its grazing grounds; counts in recent decades have found only about a thousand or so, and the state now runs conservation programmes, including protected grazing land, to save it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without this pony there would be no Manipuri polo, and arguably no modern polo.
spotlights.memory_hook: The little horse that taught the world polo.

spotlights.name: Marjing Polo Statue
spotlights.spot_it: A giant statue of a polo player on a rearing pony, on a hilltop east of Imphal.
spotlights.story_md: On Marjing hill at Heingang stands the Marjing Polo Statue, 122 feet (about 37 m) tall: a sagol kangjei player in traditional dress on a Manipuri pony, stick raised. It was unveiled on 6 January 2023 by Union Home Minister Amit Shah, at the Marjing Polo Complex dedicated to Marjing, the Meitei god of polo and horses. It is described as the world's tallest polo statue.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a public claim, in steel, that polo belongs to Manipur.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 122-foot polo player stands guard over Imphal.

spotlights.name: Yubi Lakpi, coconut rugby
spotlights.spot_it: Bare-chested men oiled up and wrestling for a greased coconut on a grass field.
spotlights.story_md: Yubi lakpi means 'snatching the coconut'. Seven players a side, oiled and wearing only shorts, fight to carry a greased coconut across a goal line, rather like rugby. Traditionally the winner offered the coconut to the king or to the deity Govindaji. Games are played at Bijoy Govinda and at Yaoshang. Some say rugby borrowed from it; there is no evidence of that, but the likeness is striking.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how much of Manipur's sport grew from ritual and festival.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rugby, but the ball is a greased coconut.

sections.title: A small state of champions
sections.intro_md:
Manipur has about 0.2% of India's people, yet it has produced a striking share of India's sporting heroes, especially women: boxers, weightlifters, footballers, archers, hockey and judo players.

Why? People point to three things. First, a culture of physical games built into festivals: polo, wrestling, boat races, martial arts. Second, a long tradition of women working in public, at the market and in protest. Third, role models: once Kunjarani Devi won world weightlifting medals in the 1990s and Dingko Singh won Asian gold in 1998, children had someone to copy. The Sports Authority of India centre at Imphal and private boxing clubs did the rest.

India's first National Sports University was set up in Imphal by an Act of Parliament in 2018.

spotlights.name: Mary Kom
spotlights.spot_it: A small, smiling boxer with a fierce guard, often in India's blue vest.
spotlights.story_md: Mangte Chungneijang Mary Kom grew up in a farming family of the Kom tribe in Kangathei, Churachandpur district. She started boxing in 2000, inspired by Dingko Singh's gold in 1998, and kept it secret from her father at first. She became the only woman to win six World Championship titles (2002, 2005, 2006, 2008, 2010 and 2018), and won bronze at the London 2012 Olympics, the first Indian woman boxer to win an Olympic medal. A Bollywood film was made about her in 2014. She received the Padma Vibhushan in 2020.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She showed that a tribal girl from a small state could become the world's best.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six world titles, and she started by hiding her gloves from her father.

spotlights.name: Saikhom Mirabai Chanu
spotlights.spot_it: A weightlifter in a red and blue suit, arms locked overhead, smiling with gold earrings shaped like Olympic rings.
spotlights.story_md: Mirabai grew up in Nongpok Kakching, Imphal East. As a girl of 12 she carried home a bundle of firewood her elder brothers had struggled to lift. At Tokyo 2020 she won silver in the 49 kg class with 202 kg (87 kg snatch, 115 kg clean and jerk), India's first medal of those Games. At Paris 2024 she finished fourth by a single kilogram. In 2025 she took silver at the World Championships in Norway, and in 2026 she won gold at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow with three Games records.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She is the current face of Manipur's extraordinary sporting output.
spotlights.memory_hook: The girl who out-carried her brothers' firewood.

spotlights.name: Ngangom Dingko Singh
spotlights.spot_it: A bantamweight boxer from Sekta, celebrated with a garland after the Bangkok Asian Games.
spotlights.story_md: Dingko Singh won gold in bantamweight boxing at the 1998 Asian Games in Bangkok, beating fighters from Thailand and Uzbekistan, India's first boxing gold at the Games in 16 years. He came from a poor family in Sekta, Imphal East, and grew up partly in an orphanage. His win sparked a boxing boom in Manipur: Mary Kom and many others trace their start to it. He received the Padma Shri in 2013 and died of cancer in 2021, aged 42.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One gold medal that created a generation of Manipuri boxers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bangkok 1998: the gold that made Mary Kom.

spotlights.name: Oinam Bembem Devi
spotlights.spot_it: A footballer in India colours, a captain's armband on her arm.
spotlights.story_md: Bembem Devi played for India's women's football team for about two decades, often as captain, and won several titles with Manipur, the most successful state side in the women's national championship. Fans called her the Durga of Indian football. She received the Arjuna Award and the Padma Shri, both in 2017, and went on to coach.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Manipur supplies a large share of India's women footballers, and she led them.
spotlights.memory_hook: Captain of India, from a state of under three million.

sections.title: Looms, pots and reeds
sections.intro_md:
In most Meitei homes there was once a loom, and many still have one. Handloom weaving is one of the largest sources of work in Manipur, mostly for women, and Manipur counts among the Indian states with the most handloom workers. Cloth is part of almost every ritual: the right phanek for a wedding, the right shawl for an honour, white for the temple.

The hills have their own crafts: Tangkhul black pottery, Kuki and Naga shawls with tribal patterns, cane and bamboo work. The valley's wetlands give kauna reed.

Several Manipur products carry Geographical Indication tags, which protect their names: the cloths Shaphee Lanphee, Wangkhei Phee and Moirang Phee, black rice (Chak-hao), the Kachai lemon, the Tamenglong orange and the Hathei chilli, and kauna craft.

spotlights.name: Longpi black pottery
spotlights.spot_it: Matte black pots and kettles with cane handles, made without a wheel.
spotlights.story_md: In Longpi (Nungbi) villages of Ukhrul district, Tangkhul potters grind a dark serpentine stone and mix it with weathered rock clay into a stiff paste. They shape it entirely by hand on a flat board, using moulds and pressure, not a potter's wheel. After firing in an open bonfire, the hot pots are rubbed with the leaves of a local tree, which gives the dark grey-black finish. Kettles, cooking pots and bowls are fitted with cane handles. Longpi ware now sells in design shops across India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of India's most distinctive pottery traditions, and a craft unique to Manipur's hills.
spotlights.memory_hook: Stone ground to clay, shaped without a wheel, polished with a leaf.

spotlights.name: Phanek
spotlights.spot_it: A wrap-around striped skirt, usually with an embroidered border, worn by Meitei women.
spotlights.story_md: The phanek is the everyday garment of Meitei women: a rectangle of cloth wrapped around the body and tucked at the waist or chest. The mayek naibi phanek has fine horizontal stripes; the most prized ones add a woven or embroidered border. Weaving is done at home on looms almost every Meitei household once had. Wearing the phanek is also political: protests often call it a symbol of Meitei identity.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the garment you see everywhere in the valley, at work, in the market and in protest.
spotlights.memory_hook: A wrap of stripes that carries a whole identity.

spotlights.name: Shaphee Lanphee
spotlights.spot_it: A dark shawl with small embroidered animals and motifs, once a warrior's honour.
spotlights.story_md: The Shaphee Lanphee is a Meitei shawl woven and embroidered with animal and other traditional motifs. In the days of the kingdom it was given by the king to warriors as an honour. The Shaphee Lanphee, the Wangkhei Phee and the Moirang Phee, Manipur's signature handloom cloths, all carry Geographical Indication tags. Moirang Phee is easy to spot: a border of repeating temple-like triangles.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Handloom is still one of the biggest sources of work in Manipur, mostly for women.
spotlights.memory_hook: A shawl once earned on the battlefield.

spotlights.name: Kauna, water-reed craft
spotlights.spot_it: Plump woven cushions, mats and baskets made of a pale, soft reed.
spotlights.story_md: Kauna is a water reed that grows in the wetlands of the Imphal Valley. Dried and woven, it makes mats, cushions, baskets and floor seating that are soft and springy. It is an eco-friendly craft with a growing market in Indian design stores. Kauna craft has been given a Geographical Indication tag, and the wetland reeds give women in lakeside villages a steady income.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns a weed of the wetlands into furniture.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sit on a lake: kauna cushions are woven from wetland reeds.

sections.title: Food: boiled, fermented, fiery
sections.intro_md:
Manipuri food is light on oil and heavy on herbs, fermentation and chilli. A typical Meitei meal is rice with a thin vegetable stew called **kangshoi** or **chamthong**, an **eromba**, fish from the lake, and a few fresh herbs on the side.

The key flavours are **ngari** (fermented fish), **hawaijar** (fermented soybean), bamboo shoot, perilla, culantro, lemon and the **u-morok**, or king chilli, one of the world's hottest. Meitei Hindus traditionally avoid meat but eat fish; hill communities eat pork, beef and smoked meats.

A big feast, a **chakluk**, is served on banana leaves, often for weddings or the Ningol Chakouba festival, with dozens of small dishes, all served in a set order. Desserts are rare; the purple chak-hao kheer is the exception.

spotlights.name: Chak-hao, black rice
spotlights.spot_it: Glutinous rice, almost black when raw, deep purple when cooked; often made into a purple pudding.
spotlights.story_md: Chak-hao means 'delicious rice' in Meiteilon. Its dark colour comes from anthocyanin, the same pigment as in blackberries. It is glutinous and cooks slowly, and Meitei families serve it at feasts as chak-hao kheer, a purple rice pudding. In 2020 Manipur's black rice received a Geographical Indication tag, and it is now exported and sold as a health food across India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best-known farm product of Manipur outside the state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Black when raw, purple when cooked, once kept for kings.

spotlights.name: Eromba
spotlights.spot_it: A thick, rough mash of boiled vegetables, fiery with chilli and pungent with fermented fish.
spotlights.story_md: Eromba is the dish most Meitei say they miss when away from home. Boiled potato, beans, bamboo shoot or greens are mashed with roasted ngari, the fermented fish, and with very hot chillies, often the u-morok, the king chilli. It is eaten with rice in small amounts, like a chutney you cannot stop eating. There is no oil and no fancy spice: the taste comes from the fish, the chilli and the herbs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the everyday core of Meitei food: boiled, fermented, hot.
spotlights.memory_hook: A mash that smells of the lake and burns like fire.

spotlights.name: Singju
spotlights.spot_it: A crunchy salad of shredded cabbage, lotus stem and herbs, tossed with roasted gram flour and chilli.
spotlights.story_md: Singju is Manipur's favourite snack salad, sold at roadside stalls in Imphal in the afternoon. Thinly sliced cabbage, lotus stem, banana flower, herbs such as perilla and culantro, and onion are tossed with roasted chickpea flour, chilli and a dash of ngari. It is crisp, spicy and slightly smoky, and often eaten with fried fritters called bora.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is how Manipur snacks: raw, green, sharp.
spotlights.memory_hook: A salad you eat at four in the afternoon with your friends.

spotlights.name: Ngari, fermented fish
spotlights.spot_it: Small dried fish packed tight in an earthen pot, fermented for months; strong smell, deep taste.
spotlights.story_md: Ngari is made from small sun-dried fish, usually the pool barb, pressed into earthen pots whose insides are coated with mustard oil, sealed and left to ferment for months. Unusually for fermented fish, no salt is added. The result is pungent and full of savoury depth, and it seasons almost everything: eromba, singju, chutneys and stews. For many outsiders ngari's smell is the first shock of a Manipuri kitchen; for Meitei it is the smell of home.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the flavour key to the whole cuisine.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fish, oil, a clay pot and patience: no salt at all.

spotlights.name: Kachai lemon
spotlights.spot_it: A large, very juicy lemon from the hills of Ukhrul, sold in sacks at a winter festival.
spotlights.story_md: Kachai is a Tangkhul village in Ukhrul district, and its lemons are famous for their juice and high vitamin C. The Kachai lemon received a Geographical Indication tag, and the village holds a Kachai Lemon Festival every winter. The lemons are sold across the North-East and used in juices, pickles and medicines at home.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how GI tags now help hill farmers sell to the rest of India.
spotlights.memory_hook: One village's lemons with their own festival.

sections.title: A year of festivals
sections.intro_md:
Manipur's calendar has festivals from every layer of its history. The Meitei year begins with **Cheiraoba** in spring, when families climb a hill to go 'higher' in the new year. Lai Haraoba follows in the summer months. The Vaishnav calendar brings Yaoshang, Rath Yatra (Kang) and Ras Lila. The hill year has Lui-Ngai-Ni, the Naga seed-sowing festival, on 15 February, and Kut, the Kuki-Zo harvest feast, on 1 November. Christmas is the biggest day in the hills.

Many festivals mix sport, dance and faith. Yaoshang is half Holi and half athletics meet. Lai Haraoba ends with wrestling. Kang, the chariot festival, comes with Thabal Chongba nights.

The ring below shows a typical year, by Gregorian month.

spotlights.name: Yaoshang
spotlights.spot_it: Five days of colours at the March full moon, with sports, bonfires and children collecting coins at roadblocks of rope.
spotlights.story_md: Yaoshang is Manipur's Holi, celebrated for five days from the full moon of Lamta (February to March). It begins with the burning of a small straw hut, the yaosang mei thaba. Children stop passers-by with ropes and ask for money, a custom called nakatheng. Every neighbourhood holds sports meets, from tug of war to races for grandmothers. Each night young people dance the Thabal Chongba, 'dancing in the moonlight', holding hands in a big circle. In the old days it was one of the few times boys and girls could openly meet.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Manipur's biggest community festival, mixing Holi with sport and courtship.
spotlights.memory_hook: Holi plus five days of sports, plus a moonlight dance.

spotlights.name: Ningol Chakouba
spotlights.spot_it: Married women in their best phaneks arriving at their parents' homes for a lavish lunch.
spotlights.story_md: Ningol Chakouba, 'the feast for married daughters', falls on the second day of the lunar month of Hiyangei, in October or November. Married women go back to their parents' home, where brothers and fathers host them to a feast and give them gifts. It is a festival of the bond between a woman and the family she left at marriage. It has spread from the Meitei to other communities, and markets are packed with gifts in the week before.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It celebrates daughters, unusual in a region with a strong pull to the husband's family.
spotlights.memory_hook: One day a year, the daughters come home and the brothers cook.

spotlights.name: Heikru Hidongba
spotlights.spot_it: Two long, narrow royal boats racing on a moat, oarsmen in turbans.
spotlights.story_md: Each September, on the eleventh day of the month of Langban, long boats called hiyang hiren race on the Bijoy Govinda moat at Sagolband in Imphal. Before the race, a garland made of heikru, Indian gooseberry, and paddy is offered for long life and prosperity. The ceremony is royal in origin, and descendants of the royal family still take part.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It keeps alive the boating culture of a valley that was once a lake.
spotlights.memory_hook: A boat race on a moat with a gooseberry garland.

spotlights.name: Kut
spotlights.spot_it: Crowds in bright Kuki-Zo shawls, a dance stage and a beauty contest, on 1 November.
spotlights.story_md: Kut is the post-harvest festival of the Kuki-Chin-Mizo peoples, celebrated across the southern hills on 1 November, a state holiday. Villages give thanks for the harvest with feasts, songs and dances, and big public events in Churachandpur and other towns include a Miss Kut contest. Since 2023 the conflict has led to smaller or cancelled public celebrations in some years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the great shared festival of the Kuki-Zo world.
spotlights.memory_hook: 1 November: harvest is in, Kut is on.

spotlights.name: Sangai Festival
spotlights.spot_it: A state tourism festival every November with cultural shows, polo and food stalls.
spotlights.story_md: The Manipur Sangai Festival, named after the dancing deer, has been held each November since 2010 to show Manipur's arts, crafts, food and sport, with venues at Hapta Kangjeibung in Imphal and in the districts. It hosts an international polo tournament, Ras Lila and Thang-Ta shows, and stalls selling black rice and Longpi pots. It was not held in 2023 after the violence began.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Manipur's main shop window for tourists.
spotlights.memory_hook: A festival named after a deer that will not attend.

sections.title: How people live: women in public
sections.intro_md:
Visitors to Manipur notice the women first: running the markets, driving scooters, leading protests, winning medals. This is not a myth. Meitei society is patrilineal, men inherit land and lead the family rituals, but women have long run trade and taken to the street. Two centuries of men being called away for war, forced labour or work built that pattern.

Daily life also has its rules. Meitei Hindu homes keep a courtyard with a tulsi plant and a household shrine to Sanamahi; shoes stay outside; fish is eaten but meat traditionally not. In the hills, the village council and the church run much of life. Across communities, respect for elders is strong, and the clan matters for marriage.

Then there is the long shadow of armed conflict. The Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, in force across much of Manipur since 1980, gave the army wide powers and legal protection. Protests against it shaped a generation.

spotlights.name: Ima Keithel, the mothers' market
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of women traders seated on raised platforms under big pagoda-style roofs, selling fish, vegetables and cloth.
spotlights.story_md: Ima Keithel, 'mothers' market', in central Imphal is run only by women, about four to five thousand of them. Only married women can hold a stall, passed down from mother to daughter. The market goes back about 500 years; it grew in the time of lalup, when men were away on forced labour or war and women ran trade. It has been a political centre too: the market women led both Nupi Lans. The present buildings, with their curving roofs, were damaged in the 2016 earthquake and repaired.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a working symbol of women's economic power in Manipur.
spotlights.memory_hook: A market where men can buy but cannot sell.

spotlights.name: Meira Paibi, the torch-bearers
spotlights.spot_it: Groups of women with lit bamboo torches marching or patrolling village lanes at night.
spotlights.story_md: Meira Paibi means 'women torch-bearers'. From the late 1970s, groups of Meitei women began patrolling their neighbourhoods at night with burning torches, at first against alcohol and drugs, and later against arrests and killings by security forces under AFSPA. On 15 July 2004, after the death of Thangjam Manorama in custody, a group of older women stood naked in front of the Assam Rifles base at Kangla holding a banner that read 'Indian Army Rape Us'. The protest shook India. Since 2023 Meira Paibi groups have also blocked roads and army convoys, which critics say has shielded armed men.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are the most powerful civil force in the valley, admired and contested.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mothers with torches: the night watch of the valley.

spotlights.name: Irom Sharmila
spotlights.spot_it: A woman with long, uncombed hair and a feeding tube taped to her nose.
spotlights.story_md: On 2 November 2000, ten civilians were shot dead at a bus stop in Malom, near Imphal airport, by Assam Rifles soldiers. Three days later Irom Sharmila, then 28, stopped eating, demanding the repeal of the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act. She was arrested for attempted suicide and force-fed through a nasal tube in a hospital ward for nearly 16 years. Amnesty International called her a prisoner of conscience. She ended her fast on 9 August 2016 and stood for election in 2017, winning 90 votes. She later married and moved to Bengaluru.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She is the world's longest-known hunger striker and the face of the AFSPA protests.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sixteen years of food through a tube, then 90 votes.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
**February 2025.** Chief Minister N. Biren Singh resigned on 9 February, and President's Rule began on 13 February. Under central rule, open fighting between Meiteis and Kukis fell sharply and many looted weapons were handed back, but few of the displaced went home.

**February 2026.** President's Rule was revoked, and on 4 February BJP leader **Yumnam Khemchand Singh** was sworn in as Chief Minister, with Nemcha Kipgen, a Kuki-Zo legislator, and Losii Dikho, a Naga, as deputy chief ministers. On 21 March he held direct talks with Kuki-Zo representatives, the first such dialogue in three years.

**April 2026.** A bomb attack on a house at Tronglaobi near Moirang killed two children on 7 April. Weeks of protest and clashes followed, and the National Investigation Agency took over the case. A new strand of tension, between Kuki and Naga groups, also flared from the village of Litan in Ukhrul district.

**Sport.** Mirabai Chanu won Commonwealth Games gold in Glasgow in 2026.

spotlights.name: The conflict since 3 May 2023
spotlights.spot_it: Burnt houses, army checkpoints between valley and hills, and relief camps in schools and halls.
spotlights.story_md: On 14 April 2023 the Manipur High Court asked the state to consider Scheduled Tribe status for the Meitei, a move tribes feared would open their protected hill land. On 3 May tribal groups held rallies against it, and clashes broke out near the border of Churachandpur and Bishnupur districts. Within days violence spread across the state. By official count, by November 2024 about 258 people had been killed, around 60,000 displaced, and some 4,786 houses burned; thousands of weapons were looted from police armouries. The valley and the Kuki-Zo hills became separated by armed buffer zones. In July 2023 a video of two Kuki women paraded naked by a mob caused national outrage.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the worst ethnic violence in India in years, and it divided the state physically.
spotlights.memory_hook: A court order, a rally, and a state split in two.

spotlights.name: Moreh and the Myanmar border
spotlights.spot_it: A busy border town of shops and warehouses, a gate and a bridge into Tamu in Myanmar.
spotlights.story_md: Moreh, on the Myanmar border about 110 km south-east of Imphal, is India's main land gateway toward Southeast Asia and part of the planned India-Myanmar-Thailand highway. For decades a Free Movement Regime let people living within 16 km on either side cross without visas, because families and tribes straddle the line. In February 2024 the Centre announced it would end that regime and fence the whole India-Myanmar border, citing drug trafficking and armed groups. Hill communities on both sides, Naga and Kuki-Zo, strongly opposed the fence.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The border is where the conflict meets geopolitics, trade and drugs.
spotlights.memory_hook: A line through families: the fence along the Myanmar border.

spotlights.name: The Jiribam to Imphal railway
spotlights.spot_it: Tall concrete piers carrying a railway across a deep gorge in the hills.
spotlights.story_md: Manipur has had almost no railway. The 111 km Jiribam to Imphal line, being built through some of India's toughest hills, will change that. It needs about 62 km of tunnels, including one of about 11.55 km, and the Noney bridge over the Ijai river, whose piers rise about 141 m, often called the world's tallest railway bridge piers. The first 55 km section to Khongsang opened in 2022. The rest was officially targeted for completion by about December 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A railway to Imphal would end the state's dependence on two vulnerable highways.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bridge pier taller than a 40-storey building, to bring trains to Imphal.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
**Myth: Manipur is a remote tribal state with no history.** Fact: the Meitei kingdom kept a royal chronicle, had its own script and fought wars with Burma; it held elections by universal adult franchise in 1948, before India did.

**Myth: polo is an English game.** Fact: the British learned it from Manipuri players in Cachar in 1859, and the first modern club was in Silchar.

**Myth: women are in charge in Manipur.** Partly true. Women dominate trade and protest, but land, inheritance and most political offices stay with men.

**Myth: the 2023 conflict is a religious war, Hindu against Christian.** Mostly false. It is ethnic and about land, identity and power. Churches and temples were both burned, churches of Meitei Christians among them, and most Naga communities, also Christian, stayed out of the Meitei-Kuki fighting.

**Myth: the sangai is extinct.** False, but close: about 260 were counted in 2016, all in one park.

sections.title: Recap: Manipur in ten lines
sections.intro_md:
1. A bowl: Imphal Valley, about 8% of the land, holds 57% of the people; 92% is hills.
2. Loktak Lake has floating islands, phumdis; Keibul Lamjao, 40 km², is the only floating national park.
3. The sangai, the dancing deer, lives wild only there: 260 in 2016.
4. The Meitei kingdom ran from Kangla; its chronicle claims a start in 33 CE.
5. 1891: Anglo-Manipur War, Tikendrajit hanged on 13 August.
6. 1944: Battle of Imphal, Japan's worst defeat until then.
7. 15 October 1949 joined India; 21 January 1972 full state.
8. Polo, Ras Lila, Pung Cholom, Thang-Ta and Meitei Mayek, the body-letter script.
9. Women run Ima Keithel; Irom Sharmila fasted 16 years against AFSPA.
10. Since 3 May 2023, Meitei-Kuki violence; President's Rule 2025; elected government back on 4 February 2026.

quiz_bank.prompt: Meitei newspapers agreed to switch from Bengali script to Meitei Mayek from January 2023.
quiz_bank.explanation: The switch date was 15 January 2023.

quiz_bank.prompt: In a Meitei home, Sanamahi, the household god, is kept in which corner?
quiz_bank.explanation: The south-west corner.

quiz_bank.prompt: Who saw Manipuri dance in Sylhet in 1919 and brought it to Santiniketan?
quiz_bank.explanation: Rabindranath Tagore.

quiz_bank.prompt: In pung cholom, the drummers dance and leap while playing.
quiz_bank.explanation: That is the whole point of it.

quiz_bank.prompt: What is Manipuri polo called in Meiteilon?
quiz_bank.explanation: Sagol kangjei, 'horse hockey'.

quiz_bank.prompt: Which medal did Mirabai Chanu win at the 2026 Commonwealth Games?
quiz_bank.explanation: Gold in the 48 kg class in Glasgow.

quiz_bank.prompt: Longpi pottery is thrown on a potter's wheel.
quiz_bank.explanation: It is shaped by hand on a board, no wheel.

quiz_bank.prompt: What is ngari?
quiz_bank.explanation: Fermented small fish, made without salt.

quiz_bank.prompt: Yaoshang is Manipur's version of which festival?
quiz_bank.explanation: Holi, over five days with sports and Thabal Chongba.

quiz_bank.prompt: Who can hold a stall at Ima Keithel?
quiz_bank.explanation: Only married women.

quiz_bank.prompt: Irom Sharmila began her fast after which event?
quiz_bank.explanation: The Malom killings of 2 November 2000.

quiz_bank.prompt: When was President's Rule imposed in Manipur?
quiz_bank.explanation: 13 February 2025, four days after Biren Singh resigned.

quiz_bank.prompt: The 2023 conflict is best described as a Hindu-Christian religious war.
quiz_bank.explanation: It is mainly an ethnic conflict over land, identity and power between Meitei and Kuki-Zo.

side_dish.title: How an island floats
side_dish.body_md:
A phumdi looks solid. You can stand on it, and fishermen build huts on it. So why does it not sink?

The answer is density. A phumdi is a tangle of living roots, dead stems and soil, held together like felt, and full of tiny spaces that hold air and the gases given off as plant matter rots. The whole mat is a little less dense than water, so it floats, but only just: about four-fifths sits below the surface, the same ratio that makes an iceberg float with most of it hidden.

Floating mats like this exist elsewhere, on lakes in Kashmir, Peru's Lake Titicaca (where the Uros people build islands of totora reed) and the Okavango in Botswana. What makes Loktak's unusual is the seasonal rhythm. In the dry months the water falls, the mats sink onto the mud and their roots take up nutrients. In the rains they lift again.

Since the Ithai barrage of 1983 held the water high all year, many phumdis never touch bottom. Scientists studying the lake say they are thinning, and thinner mats make poorer, wetter ground for the sangai. Physics and biology meet here: an island is only as strong as the cycle that feeds it.

offline_task.title: Make a quick singju
offline_task.body_md:
Singju is Manipur's afternoon salad, and you can make a version with what is in an Indian kitchen.

1. Dry-roast 3 tablespoons of besan (gram flour) in a pan on low heat until it smells nutty and turns light brown. Let it cool.
2. Slice very thin: a quarter of a cabbage, one small onion, a few leaves of coriander, and if you can find them, lotus stem or banana flower.
3. Toss with the roasted besan, crushed roasted chilli or chilli flakes, salt and a squeeze of lemon. A pinch of toasted sesame or perilla seeds is good.
4. If you can buy ngari or any dried fish, roast a few pieces and crush them in; otherwise skip it.

Eat it at once, while crisp. Notice what is missing: no oil, no tempering, almost no cooking. That is the logic of Meitei food.
